To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

student interpreters in the legal interpreting class at Auckland University of Te Piringa - Faculty of Law, had difficulty with interpreting the interrogative and declarative sentences in authentic English cross-examination questions.

(1) the Chinese language has a number of constructions which can be used to interpret interrogatives, and these constructions can result in interpretations which deviate from the source text; (2) the Chinese language also has a number of syntactical constructions which can be interpreted as tag questions; and (3) these constructions can also result in interpretations which differ from the source text.

The findings suggest that student interpreters' use of some common Chinese syntactical structures resulted in interpretations which were significantly different from the originals, involving a loss of illocutions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quality of interpreted language and its impact on the communicative effectiveness of interpreted renditions.
the development of new criteria for assessing the quality of interpreted output, and with testing these criteria on student interpreter renditions of authentic language.
the development of an assessment framework for the evaluation of student interpreter performance in legal interpreting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the student interpreters in this study had a limited ability to interpret authentic legal English into Chinese, and their performance could be significantly improved through more detailed training and practice.
student interpreters were not able to interpret the authentic English language into Chinese in the legal context in the same way as the Chinese speakers would.
student interpreters were able to produce accurate and faithful renditions of authentic cross-examination questions, but they were not able to do so in all situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have provided a framework for the analysis of interpreted texts which is based on the functionalist approaches to language, and have applied it in the context of a small number of Chinese student interpreters interpreting authentic cross examination questions in a legal interpreting classroom.

we have developed a set of criteria to evaluate the quality of the interpreted renditions of Chinese student interpreters, and we have applied this to an analysis of the interpreted rendition of authentic legal language.
the use of the criteria proposed in this study can be a useful means of evaluating the quality of the interpreted renditions produced by the student interpreters in this study.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of authentic legal texts in legal interpreting classes is a useful tool for assessing interpreter performance, and that the use of functionalist translation theory as a basis for assessment criteria can be a useful tool for testing interpreter competence.
the criteria used for assessing the quality of interpreted language should be informed by the language pair and the context in which the interpreted language is being used.

, in the context of legal interpreting in New Zealand, the use of Chinese constructions which do not correspond to English constructions can have a detrimental effect on the interpretation of legal language.
